```{r}
#| label: complete-analysis
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
df <- readr::read_csv("data/online_shoppers_intention.csv", show_col_types=FALSE)
df$Duration_Minutes <- df$ProductRelated_Duration / 60
df$Log_Duration <- log1p(df$Duration_Minutes)
df_clean <- df |>
  filter(VisitorType %in% c("New_Visitor", "Returning_Visitor")) |>
  mutate(Revenue=as.integer(Revenue),
    VisitorType=factor(VisitorType, levels=c("New_Visitor","Returning_Visitor")),
    across(c(OperatingSystems,Browser,Region,TrafficType,Month),factor),
    Weekend=factor(Weekend,levels=c(FALSE,TRUE)))
model1 <- glm(Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes + VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend,
              data=df_clean, family=binomial())
model2 <- glm(Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend,
              data=df_clean, family=binomial())

library(car)
library(pROC)
library(ResourceSelection)
dir.create("outputs/diagnostics", recursive=TRUE, showWarnings=FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size=10) + theme(panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),legend.position="bottom"))
visitor_labels <- c(New_Visitor="New visitors", Returning_Visitor="Returning visitors")
visitor_colors <- c(New_Visitor="#156082", Returning_Visitor="#BD582C")
fmt_p <- function(x) ifelse(x < .001,"<0.001",sprintf("%.3f",x))

d_assess <- df_clean
traffic_n <- table(d_assess$TrafficType)
d_assess$TrafficGroup <- factor(ifelse(traffic_n[as.character(d_assess$TrafficType)] < 100,
                                      "Other",as.character(d_assess$TrafficType)))
d_assess$Month <- relevel(d_assess$Month,"May")
stopifnot(nrow(d_assess)==12245, all(d_assess$Revenue %in% 0:1), !anyNA(d_assess))
f3 <- Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend +
  Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup
f4 <- Revenue ~ Log_Duration * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend +
  Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup
model3 <- glm(f3,data=d_assess,family=binomial())
model4 <- glm(f4,data=d_assess,family=binomial())
model3_nointer <- glm(update(f3,.~.-Duration_Minutes:VisitorType),data=d_assess,family=binomial())
model4_nointer <- glm(update(f4,.~.-Log_Duration:VisitorType),data=d_assess,family=binomial())
models_assess <- list(M1=model1,M2=model2,M3=model3,M4=model4)
null_assess <- glm(Revenue~1,data=d_assess,family=binomial())
fit_metrics <- bind_rows(lapply(names(models_assess),function(nm) {
  m<-models_assess[[nm]]
  hl<-ResourceSelection::hoslem.test(d_assess$Revenue,fitted(m),g=10)
  tibble(Model=nm,Parameters=length(coef(m)),Deviance=deviance(m),AIC=AIC(m),
    McFadden=1-as.numeric(logLik(m)/logLik(null_assess)),
    AUC=as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(d_assess$Revenue,fitted(m),levels=c(0,1),direction="<",quiet=TRUE))),
    HL_statistic=unname(hl$statistic),HL_p=hl$p.value)
}))
lrt_row <- function(label,reduced,full) {
  a<-anova(reduced,full,test="Chisq")
  tibble(Comparison=label,df=a$Df[2],LR=a$Deviance[2],p=a$`Pr(>Chi)`[2])
}
interaction_tests <- bind_rows(lrt_row("Original raw-duration model",model1,model2),
  lrt_row("Expanded raw-duration model",model3_nointer,model3),
  lrt_row("Expanded log-duration model",model4_nointer,model4))
# Raw and log-duration models are nonnested: compare AIC, not an LR test between them.
functional_tests <- fit_metrics |> filter(Model %in% c("M2","M3","M4")) |>
  select(Model,AIC,HL_p) |> mutate(Duration_form=c("Minutes","Minutes","Log(1 + minutes)"),
    Assessment="Inspect partial residual plots; no flexible-curve models fitted")
predictor_cor <- cor(d_assess[,c("Duration_Minutes","Log_Duration","ProductRelated",
                                "Administrative","Informational","ExitRates")])
vif_main <- tibble(Predictor=names(car::vif(model1)),VIF=as.numeric(car::vif(model1)))
vif_interaction <- tibble(Predictor=names(car::vif(model2)),VIF=as.numeric(car::vif(model2)))
v4<-car::vif(model4)
vif_proposed <- tibble(Term=rownames(v4),GVIF=v4[,1],df=v4[,2],adjusted_GVIF=v4[,3])
numerical_checks <- bind_rows(lapply(names(models_assess),function(nm) {
  m<-models_assess[[nm]]
  tibble(Model=nm,Converged=m$converged,Boundary=m$boundary,Rank=m$rank,
    Columns=ncol(model.matrix(m)),Max_SE=max(sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))),
    Extreme_probabilities=sum(fitted(m)<1e-8 | fitted(m)>1-1e-8))
}))
category_support <- bind_rows(lapply(c("VisitorType","Weekend","Month","TrafficGroup"),function(v) {
  d_assess |> group_by(Level=.data[[v]]) |>
    summarise(No_purchase=sum(Revenue==0),Purchase=sum(Revenue==1),.groups="drop") |>
    mutate(Variable=v,Level=as.character(Level))
}))

# Working-residual + fitted-term components are assessed on the log-odds scale.
partial_data <- function(m,xvar) {
  b<-coef(m)
  it<-grep(paste0(xvar,":VisitorType|VisitorType.*:",xvar),names(b),value=TRUE)
  slope<-b[xvar]+ifelse(d_assess$VisitorType=="Returning_Visitor",b[it],0)
  tibble(Visitor=d_assess$VisitorType,Time=d_assess[[xvar]],
    Duration_partial=residuals(m,type="working")+slope*d_assess[[xvar]],
    Page_count=d_assess$ProductRelated,
    Pages_partial=residuals(m,type="working")+b["ProductRelated"]*d_assess$ProductRelated)
}
make_partial_plot <- function(z,xlabel) {
  z |> filter(Time<=quantile(Time,.99)) |>
    ggplot(aes(Time,Duration_partial)) + geom_point(alpha=.05,size=.5,color="#777777") +
    geom_smooth(method="loess",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,color="#156082",linewidth=.8) +
    geom_smooth(method="lm",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,color="#333333",linetype=2,linewidth=.5) +
    facet_wrap(~Visitor,labeller=as_labeller(visitor_labels)) + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-5,8)) +
    labs(x=xlabel,y="Partial working residual")
}
partial_initial <- partial_data(model2,"Duration_Minutes")
partial_log <- partial_data(model4,"Log_Duration")
partial_initial_plot <- make_partial_plot(partial_initial,"Product browsing duration (minutes)")
partial_log_plot <- make_partial_plot(partial_log,"Log(1 + product browsing minutes)")
pages_partial_plot <- partial_log |> filter(Page_count<=quantile(Page_count,.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Page_count,Pages_partial)) + geom_point(alpha=.05,size=.5,color="#777777") +
  geom_smooth(method="loess",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,color="#156082",linewidth=.8) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,color="#333333",linetype=2,linewidth=.5) +
  facet_wrap(~Visitor,labeller=as_labeller(visitor_labels)) + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-5,8)) +
  labs(x="Product page count",y="Partial working residual")

diagnostic_rows <- bind_rows(lapply(c("M2","M4"),function(nm) {
  m<-models_assess[[nm]]
  tibble(Model=nm,Row=seq_len(nrow(d_assess)),Fitted=fitted(m),
    Deviance_residual=residuals(m,type="deviance"),
    Cooks_distance=cooks.distance(m),Leverage=hatvalues(m))
}))
residual_plot <- ggplot(diagnostic_rows,aes(Fitted,Deviance_residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha=.06,size=.5,color="#555555") + geom_hline(yintercept=0,linetype=2) +
  facet_wrap(~Model) + labs(x="Fitted purchase probability",y="Deviance residual")
cook_plot <- ggplot(diagnostic_rows,aes(Row,Cooks_distance)) + geom_point(alpha=.3,size=.5,color="#156082") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=4/nrow(d_assess),linetype=2,color="#BD582C") +
  facet_wrap(~Model,scales="free_y") + labs(x="Session row",y="Cook's distance")
influence_summary <- diagnostic_rows |> group_by(Model) |> summarise(
  Flagged=sum(Cooks_distance>4/nrow(d_assess)),Max_Cook=max(Cooks_distance),
  Most_influential=Row[which.max(Cooks_distance)],.groups="drop")

# Interpret a familiar time interval, combining duration and interaction terms.
duration_effect <- function(m,visitor,xvar,from=10,to=20) {
  b<-coef(m);w<-setNames(rep(0,length(b)),names(b));w[xvar]<-1
  it<-grep(paste0(xvar,":VisitorType|VisitorType.*:",xvar),names(b),value=TRUE)
  if(visitor=="Returning_Visitor") w[it]<-1
  change<-if(xvar=="Log_Duration") log1p(to)-log1p(from) else to-from
  est<-sum(w*b)*change;se<-sqrt(drop(t(w)%*%vcov(m)%*%w))*change
  tibble(Visitor=visitor,From=from,To=to,OR=exp(est),Lower=exp(est-1.96*se),
         Upper=exp(est+1.96*se),p=2*pnorm(-abs(est/se)))
}
contrast_table <- bind_rows(lapply(c("M2","M3","M4"),function(nm) {
  xvar<-if(nm=="M4") "Log_Duration" else "Duration_Minutes"
  bind_rows(lapply(levels(d_assess$VisitorType),function(v) duration_effect(models_assess[[nm]],v,xvar))) |>
    mutate(Model=nm)
}))
top5<-head(order(cooks.distance(model4),decreasing=TRUE),5)
sensitivity_models<-list("All sessions"=model4,
  "Drop largest Cook case"=glm(f4,data=d_assess[-top5[1],],family=binomial()),
  "Drop top five Cook cases"=glm(f4,data=d_assess[-top5,],family=binomial()),
  "Remove exact duplicate rows"=glm(f4,data=d_assess[!duplicated(d_assess),],family=binomial()))
sensitivity_contrasts<-bind_rows(lapply(names(sensitivity_models),function(nm) {
  bind_rows(lapply(levels(d_assess$VisitorType),function(v) duration_effect(sensitivity_models[[nm]],v,"Log_Duration"))) |>
    mutate(Analysis=nm)
}))

prediction_support <- d_assess |> filter(ProductRelated>=15,ProductRelated<=21) |>
  group_by(VisitorType) |> summarise(Sessions=n(),P95_minutes=quantile(Duration_Minutes,.95),
    Maximum_minutes=max(Duration_Minutes),Sessions_60plus=sum(Duration_Minutes>=60),.groups="drop")
prediction_grid <- expand.grid(Duration_Minutes=seq(5,25,length.out=101),VisitorType=levels(d_assess$VisitorType))
prediction_grid$VisitorType<-factor(prediction_grid$VisitorType,levels=levels(d_assess$VisitorType))
prediction_grid$Log_Duration<-log1p(prediction_grid$Duration_Minutes)
prediction_grid$ProductRelated<-18
prediction_grid$Weekend<-factor(FALSE,levels=levels(d_assess$Weekend))
prediction_grid$Administrative<-median(d_assess$Administrative)
prediction_grid$Informational<-median(d_assess$Informational)
prediction_grid$ExitRates<-median(d_assess$ExitRates)
prediction_grid$Month<-factor("May",levels=levels(d_assess$Month))
prediction_grid$TrafficGroup<-factor("2",levels=levels(d_assess$TrafficGroup))
pr<-predict(model4,newdata=prediction_grid,type="link",se.fit=TRUE)
prediction_grid$Probability<-plogis(pr$fit)
prediction_grid$Lower<-plogis(pr$fit-1.96*pr$se.fit)
prediction_grid$Upper<-plogis(pr$fit+1.96*pr$se.fit)
probability_plot <- ggplot(prediction_grid,aes(Duration_Minutes,Probability,color=VisitorType,fill=VisitorType)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=Lower,ymax=Upper),alpha=.12,color=NA) + geom_line(linewidth=.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values=visitor_colors,labels=visitor_labels) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=visitor_colors,labels=visitor_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::label_percent(accuracy=1)) +
  labs(x="Product browsing duration (minutes)",y="Purchase probability",color=NULL,fill=NULL)
calibration_data <- diagnostic_rows |> group_by(Model) |> mutate(Bin=ntile(Fitted,10)) |>
  group_by(Model,Bin) |> summarise(Predicted=mean(Fitted),Observed=mean(d_assess$Revenue[Row]),.groups="drop")
calibration_plot <- ggplot(calibration_data,aes(Predicted,Observed,color=Model)) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype=2) + geom_point(size=2) + geom_line() +
  coord_equal() + labs(x="Mean fitted probability",y="Observed conversion")
roc_objects<-lapply(models_assess[c("M2","M4")],function(m) pROC::roc(d_assess$Revenue,fitted(m),levels=c(0,1),direction="<",quiet=TRUE))
roc_data<-bind_rows(lapply(names(roc_objects),function(nm) tibble(Model=nm,FPR=1-roc_objects[[nm]]$specificities,TPR=roc_objects[[nm]]$sensitivities)))
roc_plot<-ggplot(roc_data,aes(FPR,TPR,color=Model)) + geom_line(linewidth=.8) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype=2) + coord_equal() + labs(x="1 - specificity",y="Sensitivity")
classification <- bind_rows(lapply(c(.5,mean(d_assess$Revenue)),function(t) {
  y<-d_assess$Revenue;p<-as.integer(fitted(model4)>=t)
  TP<-sum(p==1 & y==1);TN<-sum(p==0 & y==0);FP<-sum(p==1 & y==0);FN<-sum(p==0 & y==1)
  tibble(Threshold=t,TP=TP,FP=FP,FN=FN,TN=TN,Sensitivity=TP/(TP+FN),Specificity=TN/(TN+FP),Accuracy=(TP+TN)/length(y))
}))
confusion<-with(classification[1,],matrix(c(TN,FP,FN,TP),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,
  dimnames=list(Actual=c("No purchase","Purchase"),Predicted=c("No purchase","Purchase"))))

nice_term <- function(z) {
  replacements<-c("Duration_Minutes"="Duration (minutes)","Log_Duration"="Log(1 + minutes)",
    "VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor"="Returning visitor","ProductRelated"="Product page count",
    "WeekendTRUE"="Weekend vs weekday","Administrative"="Administrative page count",
    "Informational"="Informational page count","ExitRates"="Exit rate (proportion)",
    "TrafficGroupOther"="Traffic: pooled small categories","TrafficGroup"="Traffic code ","Month"="Month ","(Intercept)"="Intercept")
  for(k in names(replacements)) z<-gsub(k,replacements[[k]],z,fixed=TRUE)
  gsub(":"," x ",z,fixed=TRUE)
}
coef_table <- function(m) {
  z<-coef(summary(m));b<-z[,1];se<-z[,2]
  tibble(Predictor=nice_term(rownames(z)),`Odds ratio`=sprintf("%.4g",exp(b)),
    `SE (OR scale)`=sprintf("%.3g",exp(b)*se),
    `95% CI`=sprintf("%.3g to %.3g",exp(b-1.96*se),exp(b+1.96*se)),`p-value`=fmt_p(z[,4]))
}
table_fit <- fit_metrics |> transmute(Model,Parameters,Deviance=round(Deviance,1),AIC=round(AIC,1),
  `McFadden R2`=round(McFadden,3),`HL p`=fmt_p(HL_p))
table_contrast <- contrast_table |> transmute(Model,Visitor=dplyr::recode(Visitor,!!!visitor_labels),
  `OR: 10 to 20 min`=sprintf("%.2f",OR),`95% CI`=sprintf("%.2f to %.2f",Lower,Upper))
for(nm in c("fit_metrics","interaction_tests","functional_tests","vif_main","vif_interaction","vif_proposed",
  "numerical_checks","category_support","influence_summary","contrast_table","sensitivity_contrasts",
  "prediction_support","classification","calibration_data")) {
  write.csv(get(nm),file.path("outputs/diagnostics",paste0(nm,".csv")),row.names=FALSE)
}
write.csv(predictor_cor,"outputs/diagnostics/predictor_correlations.csv")
write.csv(coef_table(model4),"outputs/diagnostics/proposed_model_coefficients.csv",row.names=FALSE)
for(nm in c("partial_initial_plot","partial_log_plot","residual_plot","cook_plot","probability_plot","calibration_plot","roc_plot")) {
  ggsave(file.path("outputs/diagnostics",paste0(nm,".png")),get(nm),width=7,height=3.3,dpi=180,bg="white")
}
saveRDS(list(models=models_assess,fit_metrics=fit_metrics,contrasts=contrast_table),"outputs/diagnostics/model_assessment.rds")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),"outputs/diagnostics/session-info.txt")

```


# Part I. Data science memo

**To:** E-commerce product manager  
**Subject:** What browsing time tells us about new and returning shoppers

## Executive summary

We wanted to understand whether spending more time on product pages has the
same relationship with purchasing for new and returning visitors. Among 12,245
sessions, new visitors converted more often than returning visitors (24.91%
versus 13.93%), even though returning visitors spent longer browsing on average.
Our initial model suggested that additional browsing time had a stronger
positive association with purchase odds among new visitors.

That difference became less clear when we accounted for more session
characteristics and allowed the duration relationship to flatten through a log
transformation. In this adjusted model, purchase odds increased with browsing
time in both groups, but the interaction was not statistically significant
(p = `r sprintf('%.3f',interaction_tests$p[3])`). The main implication is that
time on site should be interpreted alongside the type of visitor and the rest
of the session, rather than treated as a direct measure of purchase intent.
These data do not show that keeping someone browsing longer causes a purchase.

## Why this question matters

A long visit could mean that someone is interested, comparing products or having
trouble finding information. Those possibilities suggest different product
decisions. Previous research has shown that browsing and session information
can help explain purchasing behavior (Sakar et al., 2019). We focus on whether
visitor type changes the relationship between product browsing time and
purchase conversion, after accounting for other browsing behaviors and session
characteristics.

## What we observed

```{r}
#| label: tbl-memo-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Purchase conversion and product browsing time by visitor type."
#| tbl-pos: H
df_clean |> group_by(VisitorType) |>
  summarise(Sessions=n(),Purchases=sum(Revenue),Conversion=scales::percent(mean(Revenue),accuracy=.01),
    `Mean time (min)`=round(mean(Duration_Minutes),2),.groups="drop") |>
  mutate(VisitorType=dplyr::recode(VisitorType,!!!visitor_labels)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names=c("Visitor type","Sessions","Purchases","Conversion","Mean time (min)"),booktabs=TRUE)
```

Overall, 15.45% of sessions ended in a purchase. Returning visitors spent about
twice as long on product pages on average, yet had a lower conversion rate.
These descriptive differences do not account for the composition of the
sessions, and they do not tell us whether an additional minute has the same
association with purchasing in each group.

\newpage

## Interpreting the adjusted results

```{r}
#| label: fig-adjusted-probabilities
#| fig-cap: "Adjusted log-duration model: conditional purchase probabilities with pointwise 95% confidence intervals. The profile holds product page count at 18, weekday, May, traffic code 2, other page counts and exit rate at their medians."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.55
#| fig-pos: H
probability_plot
```

Both curves rise as browsing time increases. For example, holding the other
characteristics constant, moving from 10 to 20 minutes is associated with the
following changes in purchase odds:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-memo-effects
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted purchase odds for an increase from 10 to 20 minutes (M4)."
#| tbl-pos: H
table_contrast |> filter(Model=="M4") |> select(-Model) |> knitr::kable(booktabs=TRUE)
```

The larger point estimate for new visitors does not establish that the groups'
duration associations differ; the interaction test does not provide clear
evidence of a difference. These odds ratios also apply to this particular time
interval, rather than to every additional ten minutes.

Familiarity offers one possible explanation for why browsing time could have
different meanings. New visitors may use extra time to learn about unfamiliar
products, while returning visitors may already know the site and navigate more
directly toward what they want. The initial model is consistent with this idea,
but we did not measure familiarity, browsing goals or prior purchases, and the
adjusted results do not establish that explanation. Returning visitors also
browsed longer on average in this sample. The question is what extra time
means within each group, rather than simply which group spends longer online.

## What the product team can do next

Treat browsing duration as one signal alongside page count and navigation
behavior. Investigate whether first-time visitors need clearer product
information or guidance, and whether returning visitors can easily find products
they already know. These are ideas to test, rather than effects demonstrated by
this analysis. A randomized test of a specific design change could assess its
effect on conversion. We would also collect information on shopping goals,
product categories and prior visits to better understand the patterns.

We used logistic regression with a duration-by-visitor interaction. The technical
appendix explains the additional adjustment, transformation and diagnostic
checks underlying these conclusions.

\newpage

# Part II. Technical appendix

## Data and analytical sample

The Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset contains 12,330 sessions and
18 original variables (Sakar & Kastro, 2018). Each row describes a browsing
session, and the outcome indicates whether it ended in a purchase. The source
states that sessions were selected from different users over a one-year period.
We excluded 85 sessions in the other visitor category to focus on new and
returning visitors. The resulting sample contains 12,245 sessions, including
1,892 purchases. There were no missing values requiring imputation.

The original data contain 125 duplicate rows; 121 remain in the analytical
sample. We retained them because identifiers are unavailable to determine
whether they are duplicate entries or separate sessions with identical recorded
characteristics. A sensitivity analysis removes them. Zero-duration sessions
and unusually long sessions were also retained because these values alone do
not establish a recording error. Product browsing duration was converted from
seconds to minutes. The log alternative uses $L_i=\log(1+D_i)$, retaining zero
durations.

## Models and covariate selection

Let $Y_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i)$ indicate a purchase, $D_i$ denote product
browsing minutes, and $R_i$ indicate a returning visitor. With product page
count $P_i$ and weekend indicator $W_i$, the original models are

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0+\beta_DD_i+\beta_RR_i+
\beta_PP_i+\beta_WW_i \quad (M1),$$
$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0+\beta_DD_i+\beta_RR_i+
\beta_{DR}D_iR_i+\beta_PP_i+\beta_WW_i \quad (M2).$$

M3 adds administrative and informational page counts, exit rate, month and
traffic category to M2. These variables account for other navigation, seasonality
and differences in acquisition context. They are plausible adjustment variables,
not established causal confounders. M4 retains that adjustment set and replaces
$D_i$ with $L_i$ in both the main effect and interaction:

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\gamma_LL_i+\gamma_RR_i+
\gamma_{LR}L_iR_i+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{T}\mathbf{C}_i,$$

where $\mathbf{C}_i$ contains the M3 controls. This remains an ordinary logistic
regression with one duration-by-visitor interaction. All four models use the same
sessions and are fitted by maximum likelihood.

Traffic categories with fewer than 100 sessions were pooled using their
frequencies alone to avoid very sparse levels; some original small categories
had no purchases. Reference categories are new visitors, weekdays, May and
traffic code 1. Page value was excluded because it is transaction-related.
Bounce rate was excluded because it closely overlaps exit rate. Other session
features were not all added automatically, since adjustment also changes what
the duration coefficient represents.

\newpage

## Assumptions and functional form

The binary outcome is compatible with a Bernoulli logistic model. Sampling
different users supports independence, although we cannot verify identities or
assess shared campaign and exact-date effects. Logistic regression requires an
appropriate relationship between continuous predictors and the log odds; it
does not require normally distributed predictors or residuals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-partial-log
#| fig-cap: "Partial working residuals for log duration in M4. The solid line is a smooth trend and the dashed line is a linear guide. The display omits the upper 1% of duration values and limits the vertical axis for readability; models retain all sessions."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.45
#| fig-pos: H
partial_log_plot
```

The raw-duration partial residual plots raise concerns about a constant slope,
especially across very short and long sessions. We therefore evaluated a
log-duration alternative. The transformation allows the association of an
additional minute with log odds to become smaller at longer durations. It was
not chosen simply to make the predictor less skewed. The log-duration plots
remain imperfect, so the transformation should be viewed as a useful
simplification rather than proof that the mean relationship is exactly correct.
Product page count is also assessed using a partial residual plot in the
detailed workbook.

## Correlation, VIF and numerical stability

Raw duration and product page count are strongly correlated ($r=0.861$).
In M1, their VIFs are `r round(vif_main$VIF[1],2)` and
`r round(vif_main$VIF[3],2)`. In M2, the duration and interaction term VIFs are
`r round(vif_interaction$VIF[1],1)` and `r round(vif_interaction$VIF[5],1)`.
Those higher values also reflect overlap between the duration and interaction
columns, given that most sessions are from returning visitors. Both main effects
and the interaction are retained because they define the research question.
The correlation makes holding page count fixed while changing time a more
restrictive comparison and may reduce precision.

All models converged, have full-rank design matrices and show no boundary fit.
No extremely near-zero or near-one fitted probabilities were found using
$10^{-8}$ as a screening tolerance. Both outcomes occur in the retained
categorical levels. These checks provide no obvious numerical sign of
separation, although they do not prove its absence. VIF and generalized VIF
tables, correlations and categorical support checks are exported with the
diagnostic results.

\newpage

## Residuals and influential sessions

```{r}
#| label: fig-residual-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Deviance residuals versus fitted probability for the original interaction model (M2) and expanded log-duration model (M4). Two bands are expected with a binary outcome."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 1.55
#| fig-pos: H
residual_plot
```

The two residual bands follow from observing only purchases and non-purchases;
they are not evidence of a normality violation. We assess model form alongside
these plots rather than interpreting their shape as a linear-regression
residual plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cooks-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Cook's distance. The dashed 4/n line identifies sessions to investigate, not sessions to remove automatically. Panels use different vertical scales."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 1.55
#| fig-pos: H
cook_plot
```

There are `r influence_summary$Flagged[1]` M2 sessions and
`r influence_summary$Flagged[2]` M4 sessions above $4/n$. Maximum Cook's
distances are `r round(influence_summary$Max_Cook[1],3)` and
`r round(influence_summary$Max_Cook[2],3)`, respectively. A low screening cutoff
can flag many observations in a large sample. We retain the original sample and
refit M4 after removing the largest one and five cases, rather than deleting
every flagged session. Removing exact duplicate rows is checked separately.
The 10-to-20-minute odds ratios remain close to their full-sample values in
these checks; detailed values are available in the workbook.

## Overall fit and model comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fit-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Fit comparison for the four logistic models."
#| tbl-pos: H
knitr::kable(table_fit,booktabs=TRUE)
```

M4 has the lowest AIC of these four models. Raw- and log-duration models are
nonnested, so we compare AIC rather than using an LR test between them.
McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ compares log likelihood with an intercept-only model,
rather than measuring variance explained. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test checks
calibration across ten fitted-probability groups; its nonsignificant M4 result
does not establish that all assumptions hold.

\newpage

## Interaction results and practical interpretation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-interaction-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Likelihood ratio tests of the duration-by-visitor interaction."
#| tbl-pos: H
interaction_tests |> transmute(Comparison,df,LR=round(LR,2),`p-value`=fmt_p(p)) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs=TRUE)
```

In the original M2, each additional minute is associated with about 2.55%
higher purchase odds for new visitors and 0.46% higher odds for returning
visitors, holding product page count and weekend fixed. The interaction test
supports a difference under that specification. Broader adjustment in M3 still
gives evidence of an interaction. Once duration is logged in M4, the LR
p-value is `r sprintf('%.3f',interaction_tests$p[3])`, providing weaker evidence
that the duration association differs by visitor type.

We retain the interaction in M4 to address the research question. For new
visitors, the duration slope on the log scale is $\gamma_L$; for returning
visitors it is $\gamma_L+\gamma_{LR}$. For a move from 10 to 20 minutes, each
slope is multiplied by $\log(21)-\log(11)$ and exponentiated. The intervals in
the memo account for uncertainty in the combined coefficients. Full M2 and
M4 coefficient tables are provided in the supplementary table page.

The original 60-minute illustration at 18 product pages is poorly supported:
among sessions with 15-21 product pages, no new visitor reaches 60 minutes.
The new-visitor maximum is about 43.1 minutes and its 95th percentile is 26.2.
We therefore display 5-25 minutes. The displayed probabilities remain
conditional on a specified profile; they are not visitor-group averages, and
support for every joint covariate combination remains limited.

## Brief classification assessment

M4's in-sample AUC is `r round(fit_metrics$AUC[4],3)`, compared with
`r round(fit_metrics$AUC[2],3)` for M2. At a 0.50 threshold, sensitivity is
`r scales::percent(classification$Sensitivity[1],accuracy=.1)` and specificity
is `r scales::percent(classification$Specificity[1],accuracy=.1)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "Actual outcomes (rows) versus predictions (columns), threshold 0.50."
#| tbl-pos: H
knitr::kable(confusion,booktabs=TRUE)
```

The threshold illustrates an equal-cost decision if probabilities are
calibrated; intervention costs are unavailable to choose a business optimum.
At the observed-prevalence threshold, sensitivity rises to
`r scales::percent(classification$Sensitivity[2],accuracy=.1)` and specificity
falls to `r scales::percent(classification$Specificity[2],accuracy=.1)`.
An always-no-purchase rule is already 84.55% accurate, so accuracy alone is
misleading. ROC curves and additional classification details are retained in
the workbook. These are in-sample summaries, not validated future performance.

## Limitations and future work

The analysis is observational. Shopping goals, product mix, prices and prior
purchase history were not measured. Other navigation and exit behavior may be
part of the browsing process rather than confounders, so their adjustment also
changes the interpretation. Results depend on functional form, with remaining
curvature and sparse long-duration sessions limiting a simple slope model.
The historical sample from one site and the exclusion of other visitor types
limit generalization. Model choices were evaluated on the same data, and the
reported intervals do not account for that selection. Future data should
include session identifiers, timestamps, shopping goals and product details;
randomized design changes would support stronger conclusions about conversion.

**References.** Sakar & Kastro (2018). *Online shoppers purchasing intention
dataset*. UCI. <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5F88Q>. Sakar et al. (2019).
*Neural Computing and Applications, 31*, 6893-6908.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s00521-018-3523-0>.

# Supplementary regression tables

The full tables below support the models discussed in the appendix. Large
regression tables are presented separately under the project description's
page-limit allowance. Estimates and intervals are on the odds-ratio scale;
standard errors on that scale are approximated as the odds ratio multiplied by
the coefficient's log-odds standard error. All confidence intervals are Wald
95% intervals. Reference categories are new visitors and weekdays, with May
and traffic code 1 additionally serving as references in M4. The interaction
coefficient in M4 refers to log(1 + minutes), not to one additional minute.
